reason: Connecting the arm to the breathing circulation directly addresses the first goal and links its muscles to the oxygen supply.
expectation: I expect the arm’s vessels to connect to the circulation, though the details of exchange may come later.

alternatives.reason: This seems like a useful start on tissue-fluid return, but I’ll connect the arm first.

effect: The arm is connected, and the fluid buildup shown with inadequate return makes the remaining goal clearer.
reaction: The matched tissue views make the need for a return route concrete.
reason: Connect the tissue spaces to lymphatic capillaries to begin collecting the excess fluid.
expectation: I expect fluid between cells to enter the blind-ended lymphatic vessels; the route back to blood may need another connection.

alternatives.reason: This looks like the return route into a vein, but I prefer to start where fluid enters the lymphatic system.

effect: The tissue-space fluid and proteins enter lymphatic capillaries and are then called lymph; they still need a route back to blood.
reaction: The flap-and-arrow description makes the entry point clear.
reason: Connect the draining tissue spaces to the collecting vessel to extend the return route.
expectation: I expect lymph to flow from the capillaries into the collecting vessel and toward the return duct.

alternatives.reason: Connecting the duct to the vein also advances the return route, but I prefer to follow it from the tissues outward.

effect: The collecting route now carries fluid and proteins to a duct, with the connection to the neck vein still open.
reaction: Following the arrows from tissue to duct makes the route easy to follow.
reason: Connect the duct to the venous junction to complete its route back to blood.
expectation: I expect lymph to enter the vein through the duct; the route may still need to be connected to the supplied arm.

alternatives.reason: This could connect the local drainage route to the arm, but I want to close the venous junction first.

effect: The lymphatic route now reaches a neck vein; it remains to connect the network to the supplied arm.
reaction: The continuous arrows make the return path clear.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and it should connect tissue-fluid drainage to the arm.
expectation: I expect the supplied arm to gain a lymphatic return route to the circulation, though I’m unsure whether that completes the goal.

effect: The final model connects lymph return to the supplied arm and shows how continued drainage can keep tissue fluid roughly steady. Both goals are complete.
reaction: The contrast with the earlier fluid buildup made the completed route satisfying and clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the drainage network to the arm was most worthwhile: the planned matched views link the route to its purpose, preventing fluid accumulation while filtration continues.

leastWorthwhile.text: Connecting the collecting route to the vein felt somewhat repetitive after the preceding route-building step, although it closed an important gap.

surprise.text: The tissue-space result clarified that proteins enter the lymphatic capillaries along with fluid, which is then called lymph.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless: each extended or connected the supply and return routes. The compatible-options menu guided those choices rather than requiring me to discover compatibility.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the planned buildup-and-drainage comparison gave the assembly a concrete biological consequence, though the sequence of connections was fairly predictable.
